title: The sick and the dead
hookLine: the prince asks the charioteer, and the world goes gray (Buddhacarita 3)

lines: A SICK MAN BY THE ROAD.
cards: Who is that man? A question a child might ask from the back seat of a car. The prince keeps asking it in this canto, and each answer takes something away.

First, a man by the road with a swollen belly, breathing hard, leaning on others, crying out. Then a group of men carrying something on a frame, wrapped in cloth, with people walking behind them weeping.
The palace wall has already cracked once. Now the poem widens the crack, one honest answer at a time.

teach.h: SICKNESS: CAN IT HAPPEN TO ANYONE?
teach.b: First, sickness. The charioteer explains: this man is ill. Something in his body has gone wrong, and it has brought him low.
Can it happen to anyone? Yes. The prince is shaken again, wondering how the crowds can be cheerful with this so close.
Second, death. The poem says the gods moved the charioteer to tell the truth, even though the king would rather he didn't. This man has died, he says.
He is like a log now; his family carried him out, and they are weeping.

teach.h: DEATH: IS THIS THE END FOR EVERYONE?
teach.b: Is this the end for everyone? It is. High or low, it comes to all.
Third, the gray. The same crowds, the same banners, the same gardens.

teach.h: NOTHING MOVED, BUT THE COLOR WENT.
teach.b: Nothing outside has moved, but for him the color has drained out of it. He wonders aloud how people can go about laughing and careless when death is certain and close. That astonishment has an echo in the Dhammapada.
In Max Müller's translation: "How is there laughter, how is there joy, as this world is always burning?" And fourth, where it leaves him. Not sunk.
He keeps asking, and the question has turned outward: how can a whole street laugh beside this?
That puzzle about other people, more than his own sadness, is what the next cantos follow. The garden, a friend's advice, and the night ride out of the city all grow from it.

how: Some Buddhists, especially in monastic settings, reflect regularly on sickness, aging and death as part of practice, and Buddhist funerals can include chanting on impermanence.

o: the end that comes to all, high or low
a fate that only the careless meet
a punishment for a wasted life

games.q: the sights in the poem: tap the pairs.
p: is this the end for everyone?

the poem says the gods moved him to tell it plainly.
the prince's question echoes a Dhammapada verse

games.q: you're the prince. you've just learned that death comes to everyone, and the crowds around you are laughing. what do you do?
o: join the laughter and forget it.
wonder aloud how anyone can be careless when death is close.
order the crowds to go home.
games.why: he wonders how people can laugh with death so near. the color has gone out of the parade for him.

practice: Choose one true thing you'd usually rather not think about, that someone you love will get sick one day, that this body will age, and say it to yourself plainly.

Then, instead of pushing it away, put a hand on your chest or soften your shoulders, and hold the fact the way you'd hold a frightened friend's hand. Not fixing, just holding; when the mind runs off, come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: death. The charioteer's final answer to the prince, after the sights of a sick man and a mourning procession: high or low, it comes to all. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the world goes gray. Each honest answer took something away. Day seven hundred two, done.
